title: What Is an Agent Inventory?
summary: A system of record for every agent: owner, access, permissions, lifecycle state. What the standards already require, what a real public inventory looks like, and which fields go unfilled.
body_markdown:
TL;DR


**An agent inventory is the record of every agent that exists, not just the ones somebody approved, and the hard part is not the schema. It is keeping the fields filled after launch.**


There is a public inventory you can audit yourself. OMB publishes the US federal AI use case inventory as CSV: the 2025 file holds 3,611 individually reported use cases from 41 agencies across 36 columns, with 445 flagged high-impact. The schema is good. Among those 445 high-impact entries, 318 leave the ongoing-monitoring column blank and 40 record monitoring as established.


The common reading is that inventory is a spreadsheet problem, solved once someone owns the spreadsheet. It is a freshness problem. A complete record on launch day decays into a plausible-looking guess within two quarters, and nothing in the tooling announces that it happened.


We are not saying inventory is the control. It isn't. An inventory decides nothing and blocks nothing. It is the substrate every later control reads from, which is why a stale one is worse than an obviously empty one.


What to do today: pick the three fields you would need during an incident, owner, reachable systems, and last review date, and make those three mandatory and machine-populated. Leave the other thirty optional.
